title: Mach-O Format
description: A deep dive into Apple's Mach-O binary format — headers, load commands, segments, sections, symbols, dynamic linking, dyld, code signing, and how macOS maps and runs an executable.
author: Underlayer

exercise_decls.question: What four bytes open every 64-bit Mach-O file, and what is their hex value when read as a little-endian 32-bit integer?
exercise_decls.answer: CF FA ED FE (0xFEEDFACF read little-endian)
exercise_decls.options: 7F 45 4C 46 (ELF magic)|CF FA ED FE (MH_MAGIC_64)|4D 5A (MZ)
exercise_decls.explanation: A 64-bit Mach-O file starts with bytes CF FA ED FE. Read as a little-endian uint32 this is 0xFEEDFACF (MH_MAGIC_64). 7F 45 4C 46 is ELF, 4D 5A is PE.
exercise_decls.hint1: The magic spells 'feed face' when reassembled as a 32-bit little-endian word.

exercise_decls.question: Name the four eras of Apple executables this course moves through, from oldest to newest.
exercise_decls.answer: Mach-O object files, Mach-O executables, universal (FAT) binaries, and the modern dyld-loaded binaries with chained fixups and export tries
exercise_decls.explanation: The course covers objects (MH_OBJECT), executables (MH_EXECUTE), universal FAT containers holding multiple architecture slices, and the modern format with LC_DYLD_CHAINED_FIXUPS and LC_DYLD_EXPORTS_TRIE replacing classic LC_DYLD_INFO opcodes.
exercise_decls.hint1: Think: what the compiler emits, what dyld loads, what lipo packages, and what replaced the rebase/bind opcodes.

exercise_decls.question: In a thin (non-FAT) Mach-O file, what are the four top-level regions in file order?
exercise_decls.answer: Header, load commands, segment data, __LINKEDIT
exercise_decls.options: DOS stub, PE signature, sections, imports|Header, load commands, segment data, __LINKEDIT|ELF header, program headers, sections, string table
exercise_decls.explanation: A Mach-O file starts with mach_header_64 (32 bytes), followed by the load command array, then segment/section data laid out by file offsets, and finally the __LINKEDIT segment holding symbol tables, string tables, rebase/bind opcodes, and code signatures.
exercise_decls.hint1: Unlike ELF, Mach-O does not have a DOS stub — it goes straight to the header.

exercise_decls.question: A Mach-O file begins with bytes CF FA ED FE. What is this as a 32-bit value, and what does it indicate?
exercise_decls.answer: 0xFEEDFACF (MH_MAGIC_64) — a 64-bit Mach-O file
exercise_decls.options: 0xCAFEBABE — a FAT binary|0xFEEDFACF (MH_MAGIC_64) — a 64-bit Mach-O file|0xfeedface — a 32-bit Mach-O file
exercise_decls.explanation: CF FA ED FE read little-endian is 0xFEEDFACF = MH_MAGIC_64, the magic for a 64-bit Mach-O. 0xFEEDFACE (bytes CE FA ED FE) is the 32-bit magic, and 0xCAFEBABE is FAT_MAGIC (big-endian).
exercise_decls.hint1: Read the four bytes as a little-endian uint32 and match against the three magics.

exercise_decls.question: How many bytes is mach_header_64, and which field comes last?
exercise_decls.answer: 32 bytes; reserved (uint32) comes last
exercise_decls.options: 28 bytes; flags comes last|32 bytes; reserved (uint32) comes last|40 bytes; reserved comes last
exercise_decls.explanation: mach_header_64 = magic(4) + cputype(4) + cpusubtype(4) + filetype(4) + ncmds(4) + sizeofcmds(4) + flags(4) + reserved(4) = 32 bytes. The reserved field exists only in the 64-bit variant.
exercise_decls.hint1: 32-bit mach_header is 28 bytes; the 64-bit version adds one uint32.

exercise_decls.question: A Mach-O header has ncmds = 18 and sizeofcmds = 2016. What do these two fields control?
exercise_decls.answer: ncmds = number of load commands; sizeofcmds = total byte size of all load commands after the header
exercise_decls.options: ncmds = number of sections; sizeofcmds = file size|ncmds = number of load commands; sizeofcmds = total byte size of all load commands after the header|ncmds = number of segments; sizeofcmds = __LINKEDIT size
exercise_decls.explanation: ncmds tells the loader how many load commands to walk; sizeofcmds gives the total bytes those commands occupy (so the first segment's data starts at 32 + sizeofcmds). Both are set by the linker and must be consistent with the actual command stream.
exercise_decls.hint1: The loader needs both a count and a byte size to safely walk the array.

exercise_decls.question: What are the cputype values for x86_64 and arm64 in a Mach-O header?
exercise_decls.explanation: CPU_TYPE_X86_64 = 0x01000007 (CPU_TYPE_X86 | CPU_ARCH_ABI64), CPU_TYPE_ARM64 = 0x0100000C (CPU_TYPE_ARM | CPU_ARCH_ABI64). 0x8664 and 0xAA64 are PE machine values, not Mach-O cputypes. 3 and 0 are cpusubtype values.
exercise_decls.hint1: Both are 32-bit values with the ABI64 bit set in the high byte.

exercise_decls.question: A FAT binary starts with bytes CA FE BA BE. What does this indicate, and why is it big-endian?
exercise_decls.answer: FAT_MAGIC — a universal binary; it is big-endian so the reader can determine byte order before knowing the slice architecture
exercise_decls.options: MH_MAGIC_64 — 64-bit file|FAT_MAGIC — a universal binary; it is big-endian so the reader can determine byte order before knowing the slice architecture|A Java class file — not Mach-O
exercise_decls.explanation: CA FE BA BE (big-endian 0xCAFEBABE) is FAT_MAGIC. The fat_header and fat_arch fields are always big-endian regardless of the slice architectures, so the loader can read nfat_arch and locate each slice before knowing whether that slice is x86_64 or arm64.
exercise_decls.hint1: The magic itself tells you the byte order convention for the container.

exercise_decls.question: Each load command starts with which two fields, and what does the second control?
exercise_decls.answer: cmd (uint32) and cmdsize (uint32); cmdsize gives the total bytes of this command including its payload
exercise_decls.options: cmd and ncmds; ncmds is the count|cmd (uint32) and cmdsize (uint32); cmdsize gives the total bytes of this command including its payload|cmdsize and flags; flags selects the command type
exercise_decls.explanation: Every load_command begins with cmd (identifying the type, e.g. 0x19 = LC_SEGMENT_64) and cmdsize (the full byte length of this command). The loader advances by cmdsize to reach the next command — this is how variable-length commands are walked safely.
exercise_decls.hint1: The loader needs both an ID and a length to step through the array.

exercise_decls.question: A segment has vmsize = 0xC000 but filesize = 0x4000. What does this difference mean?
exercise_decls.answer: The last 0x8000 bytes are zero-filled in memory (bss-like) — they occupy no file space
exercise_decls.options: The file is truncated and the segment is invalid|The last 0x8000 bytes are zero-filled in memory (bss-like) — they occupy no file space|The segment spans two files
exercise_decls.explanation: When vmsize exceeds filesize, the extra bytes are mapped as zero-fill — like .bss in ELF. The __DATA segment of libasyncProfiler.dylib shows this: vmsize 0xC000 but filesize 0x4000, so 0x8000 bytes of zero-fill (.bss, .common) cost no disk space.
exercise_decls.hint1: Think about where uninitialized globals live.

exercise_decls.question: What are the vmaddr, fileoff, and filesize of the __PAGEZERO segment in a typical 64-bit executable?
exercise_decls.answer: vmaddr = 0, vmsize = 0x100000000 (4 GiB), fileoff = 0, filesize = 0
exercise_decls.options: vmaddr = 0x100000000, fileoff = 0, filesize = 0x1000|vmaddr = 0, vmsize = 0x100000000 (4 GiB), fileoff = 0, filesize = 0|No such segment exists
exercise_decls.explanation: __PAGEZERO maps 4 GiB of unmapped memory at address 0 with no file backing (filesize = 0). It exists so that null-pointer dereferences fault — the loader maps it with no permissions (prot = 0).
exercise_decls.hint1: Its whole purpose is to make address 0 unmapped.

exercise_decls.question: How many bytes is section_64, and what field gives its file offset?
exercise_decls.answer: 80 bytes; the offset field is 'offset' (uint32)
exercise_decls.options: 40 bytes; PointerToRawData|80 bytes; the offset field is 'offset' (uint32)|64 bytes; VirtualAddress
exercise_decls.explanation: section_64 = 80 bytes: sectname(16) + segname(16) + addr(8) + size(8) + offset(4) + align(4) + reloff(4) + nreloc(4) + flags(4) + reserved1(4) + reserved2(4) + reserved3(4). The 'offset' field is the file offset of the section's data.
exercise_decls.hint1: Two 16-byte name fields plus addr/size as 64-bit values.

exercise_decls.question: LC_SYMTAB points to the symbol table. What three pieces of data does it reference?
exercise_decls.answer: Symbol array (symoff/nsyms), string table (stroff/strsize)
exercise_decls.options: Section headers, relocation entries, string table|Symbol array (symoff/nsyms), string table (stroff/strsize)|Export trie, import table, GOT
exercise_decls.explanation: LC_SYMTAB has symoff + nsyms (the nlist_64 array) and stroff + strsize (the string table). Each nlist_64's n_strx is an offset into the string table. (The fourth pair, extreloff/nextrel, is unused in 64-bit — external relocations live in the object file's section headers.)
exercise_decls.hint1: Symbols plus their names.

exercise_decls.question: In LC_DYSYMTAB, what do ilocalsym/nlocalsym, iextdefsym/nextdefsym, and iundefsym/nundefsym define?
exercise_decls.answer: Index/count ranges partitioning the symbol table into local, external-defined, and external-undefined symbols
exercise_decls.options: File offsets into __LINKEDIT|Index/count ranges partitioning the symbol table into local, external-defined, and external-undefined symbols|Virtual addresses of the three symbol kinds
exercise_decls.explanation: The symbol table is partitioned: local symbols first (ilocalsym..), then externally-defined symbols, then externally-undefined (imported) symbols. dyld uses these ranges to build its symbol tables without scanning all nsyms entries.
exercise_decls.hint1: iloc = index of local, next = number of external-defined, iundef = index of undefined.

exercise_decls.question: How many bytes is one relocation_info entry in a 64-bit Mach-O object file?
exercise_decls.answer: 8 bytes: r_address (int32) + a packed bitfield uint32
exercise_decls.options: 4 bytes: just r_address|8 bytes: r_address (int32) + a packed bitfield uint32|16 bytes: two int64s
exercise_decls.explanation: relocation_info = 8 bytes: r_address (4 bytes, the section offset being relocated) followed by a 4-byte packed field containing r_symbolnum (24 bits), r_pcrel (1), r_length (2), r_extern (1), r_type (4).
exercise_decls.hint1: 32-bit address plus 32-bit flags = 8 bytes.

exercise_decls.question: In LC_LOAD_DYLIB, what field holds the library's install name, and what does an ordinal mean?
exercise_decls.answer: dylib.name.offset points to a string (e.g. /usr/lib/libSystem.B.dylib); the ordinal is the 1-based index of this dylib in the load-command list
exercise_decls.options: dylib.name.offset points to a string; the ordinal is a hash of the name|dylib.name.offset points to a string (e.g. /usr/lib/libSystem.B.dylib); the ordinal is the 1-based index of this dylib in the load-command list|There is no name — only a UUID
exercise_decls.explanation: LC_LOAD_DYLIB stores dylib.name.offset (file offset of a null-terminated install name) plus timestamp, current_version, compatibility_version. Bind opcodes use SET_DYLIB_ORDINAL_IMM with a 1-based ordinal counting LC_LOAD_DYLIB/LC_LOAD_WEAK_DYLIB/LC_REEXPORT_DYLIB commands in order.
exercise_decls.hint1: dyld resolves bind opcodes by ordinal, not by name.

exercise_decls.question: What does LC_DYLD_INFO_ONLY provide that LC_DYLD_INFO does not?
exercise_decls.answer: The ONLY variant is required by dyld — LC_DYLD_INFO without ONLY is treated as optional/ignored by modern dyld
exercise_decls.options: Nothing — they are identical|The ONLY variant is required by dyld — LC_DYLD_INFO without ONLY is treated as optional/ignored by modern dyld|The ONLY variant includes export trie; the plain one does not
exercise_decls.explanation: LC_DYLD_INFO_ONLY = 0x80000022 has the LC_REQ_DYLD bit set (0x80000000), meaning dyld requires it and will refuse to load the binary if it cannot understand it. Plain LC_DYLD_INFO (0x22) lacks that bit and is treated as a hint modern dyld may ignore.
exercise_decls.hint1: The high bit in the cmd value is LC_REQ_DYLD.

exercise_decls.question: What data structure does LC_DYLD_EXPORTS_TRIE point to, and why is it a trie?
exercise_decls.answer: A byte trie where each edge is a string fragment; edges share prefixes so lookup is a single walk from the root
exercise_decls.options: A sorted array of names for binary search|A byte trie where each edge is a string fragment; edges share prefixes so lookup is a single walk from the root|A hash table with open addressing
exercise_decls.explanation: The export trie is a byte-encoded tree: each node has an optional terminal (export flags + address) and children with label edges. Shared prefixes compress the export list — dyld walks edge-by-edge looking up a symbol name in one pass. It replaced the flat export name array from LC_DYLD_INFO.
exercise_decls.hint1: Think about how you'd share prefixes like __ZNS and __ZNSo.

exercise_decls.question: What does LC_DYLD_CHAINED_FIXUPS replace, and what is its core idea?
exercise_decls.answer: It replaces separate rebase/bind opcode streams; it chains fixup locations through the pointers themselves (each pointer holds a small delta to the next)
exercise_decls.options: It replaces the export trie; pointers are sorted alphabetically|It replaces separate rebase/bind opcode streams; it chains fixup locations through the pointers themselves (each pointer holds a small delta to the next)|It replaces __LINKEDIT entirely
exercise_decls.explanation: Chained fixups encode rebase/bind info as a linked list threaded through the pointer slots themselves. Each 64-bit pointer packs a small next-chain offset in its low bits, so dyld follows the chain in-place instead of reading a separate opcode stream. LC_DYLD_CHAINED_FIXUPS points at dyld_chained_fixups_header in __LINKEDIT.
exercise_decls.hint1: The pointers point at each other.

exercise_decls.question: How does dyld find the entry point of a modern Mach-O executable?
exercise_decls.answer: LC_MAIN.entryoff — a file offset from the start of the image to the entry instruction
exercise_decls.options: The first byte of __text|LC_MAIN.entryoff — a file offset from the start of the image to the entry instruction|A fixed address like 0x100000000
exercise_decls.explanation: LC_MAIN (0x80000028) carries entryoff (file offset of _main) and stacksize. dyld adds the image's vmaddr base to convert it to a runtime address. Older binaries used LC_UNIXTHREAD to embed the entry address directly in a thread state struct.
exercise_decls.hint1: It is a file offset, not a virtual address — dyld adds the slide.

exercise_decls.question: What three pieces of version information does LC_BUILD_VERSION carry, and what are platforms 1 and 2?
exercise_decls.answer: platform, minos (minimum OS), sdk (SDK built with); platform 1 = macOS, platform 2 = iOS
exercise_decls.options: Timestamp, checksum, signature; platform 1 = 32-bit, 2 = 64-bit|platform, minos (minimum OS), sdk (SDK built with); platform 1 = macOS, platform 2 = iOS|Entry point, stack size, heap size; 1 = kernel, 2 = user
exercise_decls.explanation: LC_BUILD_VERSION (0x32) holds platform (1 = PLATFORM_MACOS, 2 = PLATFORM_IOS), minos (minimum OS version required), and sdk (SDK version used to build). It replaced the older LC_VERSION_MIN_MACOSX for newer toolchains.
exercise_decls.hint1: Think: where it runs and what it was built against.

exercise_decls.question: What does LC_CODE_SIGNATURE point to, and what is the outermost structure called?
exercise_decls.answer: A blob in __LINKEDIT; the outermost structure is a superblob (magic 0xFADE0CC0)
exercise_decls.options: An ELF note segment|A blob in __LINKEDIT; the outermost structure is a superblob (magic 0xFADE0CC0)|The export trie
exercise_decls.explanation: LC_CODE_SIGNATURE is a linkedit_data_command holding dataoff/datasize pointing at a code signature blob in __LINKEDIT. The blob starts with a superblob header (magic 0xFADE0CC0, length, count) indexing embedded blobs: code directory (0xFADE0C02), requirements, entitlements, and the DER signature.
exercise_decls.hint1: Code signatures live at the end of __LINKEDIT, referenced by a load command.

exercise_decls.question: Where does a Mach-O executable store DWARF debug information?
exercise_decls.answer: In separate .dSYM bundles — the main binary keeps only UUID and debug links
exercise_decls.options: In a .debug section inside the binary|In separate .dSYM bundles — the main binary keeps only UUID and debug links|In the symbol table's string table
exercise_decls.explanation: macOS uses dSYM companion bundles: the main binary keeps LC_UUID (which the dSYM also carries) plus minimal debug hints, while full DWARF sections live in the .dSYM/Contents/Resources/DWARF/<name> file. dsymutil matches them by UUID.
exercise_decls.hint1: The UUID in LC_UUID is the join key.

exercise_decls.question: What security purpose does __PAGEZERO serve beyond catching null dereferences?
exercise_decls.answer: It occupies the low 4 GiB so no code or data can be mapped there, blocking NULL-page exploits
exercise_decls.options: It stores the stack canary|It occupies the low 4 GiB so no code or data can be mapped there, blocking NULL-page exploits|It holds imported symbol names
exercise_decls.explanation: Beyond null-pointer faults, __PAGEZERO prevents any attacker-mapped page from living at low addresses — classic exploits that mmap at address 0 or low addresses are blocked because the loader already reserved that range with no permissions (prot = 0/0).
exercise_decls.hint1: Think about what used to be mappable at address 0.

exercise_decls.question: What is dyld, and what does it do before transferring control to LC_MAIN.entryoff?
exercise_decls.answer: The macOS dynamic linker — it maps the binary, resolves binds/rebases via chained fixups or opcodes, loads dependent dylibs, runs initializers, then jumps to the entry point
exercise_decls.options: The kernel scheduler|The macOS dynamic linker — it maps the binary, resolves binds/rebases via chained fixups or opcodes, loads dependent dylibs, runs initializers, then jumps to the entry point|The code-signing daemon
exercise_decls.explanation: dyld is macOS's equivalent of ld.so: it maps the executable and its dylib dependencies, applies rebasing and binding (via chained fixups or classic opcodes), runs LC_ROUTINES/mod-init callbacks, then transfers control to LC_MAIN.entryoff. Only after all that does your main() run.
exercise_decls.hint1: It is the first user-mode code that runs in a Mach-O process.

exercise_decls.question: In a 64-bit Mach-O executable's memory map, what is the typical address of __TEXT and why?
exercise_decls.answer: 0x100000000 (4 GiB) — chosen to stay out of the low 4 GiB reserved by __PAGEZERO
exercise_decls.options: 0x00000000 — starts at address zero|0x100000000 (4 GiB) — chosen to stay out of the low 4 GiB reserved by __PAGEZERO|0x7FFFFFFF000 — top of user space
exercise_decls.explanation: With __PAGEZERO consuming 0x0..0x100000000, __TEXT begins at 0x100000000. This gives a huge ASLR-friendly base while keeping NULL-page protection. PIE binaries slide from this base at load time.
exercise_decls.hint1: Add __PAGEZERO's vmsize to its vmaddr.

exercise_decls.question: Trace the path from dyld receiving control to your C main() running in a modern Mach-O executable.
exercise_decls.answer: dyld maps segments → applies chained fixups (rebase/bind) → loads dependent dylibs recursively → runs mod-init functions → jumps to LC_MAIN.entryoff → CRT startup runs → main() is called
exercise_decls.explanation: dyld first maps __PAGEZERO/__TEXT/__DATA/__LINKEDIT with correct protections, then walks chained fixups (or LC_DYLD_INFO opcodes) to slide pointers and resolve binds, recursively loads LC_LOAD_DYLIB dependencies, runs constructors, and finally jumps to entryoff. The entry stub sets up the stack and calls the C runtime, which calls main().
exercise_decls.hint1: Map, fix up, load deps, constructors, entry, CRT, main.
